title: On the difference between knowing a system and understanding it
excerpt: You can spend a year on a codebase and still not understand it. Understanding is about mental models, not familiarity.
body:
You can spend a year working on a codebase and still not understand it. This is one of the more uncomfortable truths in software engineering, and it is worth sitting with rather than explaining away.

Familiarity is not a model

Knowing a system means being able to navigate it. You know which files to open, which engineers wrote which parts, which configurations control which behaviours. This knowledge is real and valuable. But it is not the same as having a coherent mental model of how the system works.

Understanding a system means being able to predict its behaviour under novel conditions. It means being able to reason about what will happen when a new load pattern arrives, or when a dependency changes its interface, or when two subsystems that have never interacted before suddenly need to. That kind of reasoning requires a model — not just familiarity.

Why this matters for architecture

Good architectural decisions require understanding, not just knowledge. When an engineer who knows a system is asked to extend it, they will follow the existing patterns whether or not those patterns are good. When an engineer who understands a system is asked to extend it, they can make a genuine judgment about whether the existing patterns serve the new requirement — or whether this is the right moment to change direction.

Building this understanding is slow and cannot be shortcut. It comes from reading code until you can explain it without looking at it, from tracing execution paths under failure conditions, and from asking why a design is the way it is until you have a satisfying answer. It is some of the most valuable work an engineer can do.
